unit.title: Perform advanced welding using oxyacetylene welding process (OAW)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which document tells you the joint, filler rod, nozzle size and technique to use for a weld?
options: The delivery note that came with the gas cylinders
The Centre's fire plan and list of emergency numbers
The welding procedure sheet for the job
The wiring diagram on the side of the machine

questions.stem: Which eye protection is suitable for oxy-acetylene welding of 3 mm steel sheet?
options: Gas welding goggles with about a shade 5 filter
An arc welding helmet with a shade 12 filter
Clear safety glasses with no filter at all
Dark sunglasses with good plastic lenses

questions.stem: When welding overhead, which extra protection is most important?
options: Shorts, so that heat can escape from the legs
Thin rubber gloves, so that you get a better grip on the rod
Ear plugs, worn instead of goggles
A cap, and a collar buttoned up against falling hot metal

questions.stem: Why must oxygen never be used to freshen the air in a tank or a small room?
options: Oxygen is a poison that harms the lungs at once
Extra oxygen makes clothes and hair catch fire very easily
Oxygen is much heavier than air and pushes the air out
Oxygen turns into acetylene when it meets warm air

questions.stem: Why must copper pipe never be used to carry acetylene?
options: Copper makes the acetylene leak out much faster
Acetylene and copper can form a compound that explodes
Copper pipe is too heavy to fix to the workshop wall
Copper cools the gas so that it will not light at the torch

questions.stem: Where is the hottest part of a neutral oxy-acetylene flame?
options: Just in front of the tip of the inner cone
At the very end of the outer flame
Right at the face of the nozzle
In the middle of the large outer flame envelope

questions.stem: About how hot is a neutral oxy-acetylene flame at its hottest point?
options: About 900 °C
About 1500 °C
About 3100 °C
About 6000 °C

questions.stem: How do you choose the nozzle size for an oxy-acetylene weld?
options: Always use the largest nozzle so the work goes faster
Use the nozzle that was left on the torch last time
Choose the smallest nozzle so that less gas is used
By the metal and its thickness, from the maker's chart

questions.stem: What is a hose check valve (non-return valve) for?
options: It stops gas flowing back up the hose the wrong way
It shows the pressure of the gas left in the hose
It lowers the cylinder pressure to working pressure
It mixes the two gases before they reach the nozzle

questions.stem: In what order are the torch valves opened when lighting an oxy-acetylene torch?
options: Oxygen first and light it, then add the acetylene
Both valves together, then light the mixed gas
Acetylene first and light it, then add the oxygen
Oxygen fully open, then the acetylene, then light

questions.stem: Which flame is used for fusion welding mild steel?
options: Oxidising flame
Carburising flame
Acetylene-only flame
Neutral flame

questions.stem: Which flame is normally used for braze welding (bronze welding) steel with a brass filler rod?
options: Strongly carburising
Slightly oxidising
Acetylene only, no oxygen
Neutral with a long feather

questions.stem: What happens when mild steel is welded with an oxidising flame?
options: The pool sparks and foams, leaving a brittle, porous weld
The weld becomes extra strong, smooth and tough all through
The weld is a little harder but otherwise sound
Nothing changes, because flame type does not matter

questions.stem: Why are mild steel gas welding rods copper coated?
options: To add copper to the weld and make it stronger
To make the rods carry electricity like an electrode
To protect them from rusting while they are stored
To act as a flux and clean the weld pool

questions.stem: How should the filler rod be used while welding?
options: Held well away from the flame until the pool is ready
Pressed hard onto the cold metal ahead of the pool
Melted by the inner cone and dripped onto the plate
Its hot end kept in the outer flame and dipped into the pool

questions.stem: When is a flux needed in oxy-acetylene work?
options: For every weld on clean mild steel
For cast iron, aluminium and braze welding
Only for welds in the overhead position
Never, as flux is only used for arc welding

questions.stem: In leftward (forehand) welding, which way does the flame point?
options: Forward, towards the part of the joint not yet welded
Back over the weld that has just been made
Straight down at 90° to the plate, without tilting it at all
Out to one side, away from the line of the joint

questions.stem: Leftward welding of steel is normally used for which thickness of metal?
options: Only plate over 25 mm thick
Plate between 10 mm and 20 mm
Thin sheet, up to about 5 mm
Any thickness; it makes no difference

questions.stem: What is one advantage of rightward (backhand) welding on thicker steel plate?
options: It gives the neatest finish on very thin sheet
It needs no filler rod at all, only the flame
It works best with a strongly carburising flame
It needs a smaller joint angle and is faster

questions.stem: How far should the tip of the inner cone be held from the weld pool?
options: Dipped right into the weld pool
About 2–3 mm, not touching
About 25 mm away
About 50 mm away

questions.stem: Which sign shows that a butt weld has full penetration?
options: A high, rounded bead on the top face only
Spatter spread all over the plate surface
An even, small bead along the back (root) side
A dark colour along both sides of the joint

questions.stem: Which edge preparation is usual for a butt weld in 1.6 mm steel sheet?
options: Square edges, close together or with a very small gap
A 60° V on each sheet, with a 3 mm root face
A double-V on both sides, with a wide root gap
A U-groove machined along the full edge of each of the sheets

questions.stem: Why are sheet butt joints tacked at short, even spaces before welding?
options: To use up short pieces of filler rod
To heat the sheets up slowly before the main weld
To mark where each new rod should start
To hold the gap and stop the edges moving

questions.stem: What must be cleaned off the joint before gas welding?
options: Only the loose dust, because the flame burns off all the rest
Rust, mill scale, paint, oil and dirt, back to bright metal
Nothing, because the flux will clean the joint
Only paint, because rust helps the weld flow

questions.stem: What does position 3G mean?
options: A butt weld in the vertical position
A butt weld in the flat position
A fillet weld in the overhead position
A pipe weld with the pipe being rolled

questions.stem: In the 5G pipe position, how is the pipe set up?
options: Axis vertical and fixed, welded around the side
Axis horizontal, with the pipe rolled as you weld
Axis horizontal and fixed, welded all round
Axis at 45° and fixed, welded all round

questions.stem: When welding vertically upward, how do you stop the pool from sagging?
options: Use a bigger nozzle and make a larger pool
Point the flame down to push the pool back
Weld much faster and add no filler rod
Keep the pool small and point the flame upward

questions.stem: Why is a smaller weld pool used in overhead welding?
options: A small pool uses less gas and filler rod
A small pool is held up by surface tension; a big one drips
A small pool makes the weld look neater when seen from below
A small pool cools slowly and stays soft longer

questions.stem: In a horizontal butt weld (2G) on a vertical plate, which fault is most common?
options: Sagging of the pool, with undercut on the top edge
Too much penetration at the start only
Cracking of the filler rod as it is used
A carburised, hard layer on the bottom edge

questions.stem: How many tack welds are usual on a small-bore pipe butt joint before welding?
options: One tack, at the top of the pipe
None; the pipe is held by hand
Three or four, evenly spaced
One every 10 mm all the way round

questions.stem: When welding a fixed horizontal pipe (5G) uphill, where is each half of the weld started?
options: At the top, working down each side to the bottom
At the 3 o'clock point, going right round in one run
Anywhere, because the pipe is turned as you weld
At the bottom, working up each side to the top

questions.stem: Why is cast iron preheated and cooled slowly when it is gas welded?
options: To make it melt at a lower temperature than usual
To stop it cracking from uneven heating and cooling
To burn off the carbon so that it becomes mild steel
To make the flux work without any filler rod

questions.stem: Why is aluminium hard for a beginner to gas weld?
options: It shows no colour change before it melts and collapses
It melts at a much higher temperature than steel does
It cannot be welded with any kind of flame at all
It burns away like paper as soon as the flame touches it

questions.stem: After gas welding aluminium with flux, what must be done?
options: Leave the flux on, to protect the weld from rust and dirt
Paint over the flux at once to seal it in
Wash all the flux off with hot water and a brush
Grind the flux into the surface with a disc

questions.stem: In braze welding (bronze welding) of steel, what happens to the steel itself?
options: It melts and mixes fully with the bronze rod
It is melted first, then the bronze is added
It is not heated at all; only the bronze rod is heated up
It is heated but not melted, and the bronze bonds to it

questions.stem: What is lack of fusion?
options: A weld that is wider than the drawing shows
Weld metal lying on the edge without melting into it
A weld with far too much penetration
Small holes left in the weld by trapped gas

questions.stem: What usually causes burn-through (holes) in thin sheet?
options: Too much heat: nozzle too big or travel too slow
Too little heat: nozzle too small or travel too fast
Using a neutral flame instead of a carburising one
Cleaning the joint back to bright metal first

questions.stem: What is undercut?
options: Weld metal piled too high on the joint face
A crack running along the middle of the weld
A groove melted at the weld edge and left unfilled
A weld that is shorter than the drawing asks for

questions.stem: Which fault is often caused by dirt, paint or an oxidising flame?
options: Undercut at the toes
Excess root penetration
Misalignment of plates
Porosity (gas holes)

questions.stem: What does a root bend test show?
options: How hard the face of the weld is, by filing it
Whether the root fused, bent with the root on the outside
How much the weld weighs compared with the plate
Whether the weld is the right width, by measuring it with a rule

questions.stem: What check is made first on every finished weld?
options: A visual check of its size, shape and surface faults
A bend test on every single weld before it is put into use
An X-ray of every weld before it is painted
A hardness test on the face with a file

questions.stem: Which method helps to reduce distortion when gas welding thin sheet?
options: Use a bigger nozzle and weld more slowly
Weld the whole seam in one long run, without any tacks
Tack closely, clamp it, and use a back-step sequence
Heat the whole sheet red hot before you start

questions.stem: Why does gas welding usually cause more distortion in sheet than arc welding?
options: The gas flame is much hotter than any welding arc
Gas welding always uses much thicker filler rods than arc
The gas pushes on the sheet and bends it
It is slower, so the heat spreads over a wider area

questions.stem: You stop welding for a few minutes. What should you do with the torch?
options: Leave it lit, pointing down at the floor
Shut it off and hang it up away from the cylinders
Lay it on the cylinder trolley, still lit and ready to use
Hang it, still lit, on the regulator

questions.stem: After bleeding the lines, a regulator gauge needle does not go back to zero. What should you do?
options: Tag the regulator out of use and report it
Tap the gauge with a spanner until it moves
Keep using it but add 50 kPa to each reading
Oil the gauge so that the needle moves freely

essays.stem: Describe the main hazards of oxy-acetylene welding, and how each one is controlled.
essays.modelAnswer: Fire and explosion: acetylene burns very easily and oxygen makes other materials burn fiercely. To control this, keep cylinders upright and chained, check for leaks with leak-detection solution, fit flashback arrestors and check valves, use acetylene below about 100 kPa (15 psi), keep oil and grease off oxygen fittings, and clear anything that can burn from the area, with an extinguisher ready. Burns: the flame, the hot metal and the sparks can burn badly. Wear leather gloves, flame-resistant long sleeves and boots, use tongs, and mark hot work. Eye damage: the bright flame and pool give glare and infrared light. Wear gas welding goggles with about a shade 4–6 filter. Fumes: heating paint, zinc coatings, oil and some fluxes gives harmful fumes. Clean the metal first and work with good ventilation or extraction, with a respirator when needed. Flashback and backfire: use the right pressures, a clean nozzle and the right lighting order. Always follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Fire and explosion, with controls (leak test, arrestors, chained upright cylinders, acetylene below about 100 kPa, no oil on oxygen fittings)
Burns, with controls (gloves, flame-resistant clothing, tongs, hot metal marked)
Eye damage, with control (gas welding goggles about shade 4–6)
Fumes, with controls (clean metal, ventilation or extraction, respirator)
Area fire precautions and following the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

essays.stem: Describe how to check and assemble an oxy-acetylene welding outfit, and test it for leaks, before you start welding.
essays.modelAnswer: Check that both cylinders are chained upright and hold the right gases, and that the valves and outlets are clean and free from oil, grease and damage. Check the regulators for cracked glass, bent needles and damaged threads, and make sure the adjusting screws are wound out. Fit the oxygen regulator (right-hand thread) and the acetylene regulator (left-hand thread) firmly with the right spanner. Fit flashback arrestors at the regulator outlets. Inspect the hoses along their whole length for cuts, burns, cracks and worn ends, then connect them the right way round, with check valves where they join the torch. Choose the nozzle from the maker's chart for the metal thickness, and check that it is clean and its seat is not damaged. Stand to one side and open the cylinder valves slowly, then set the working pressures. Brush leak-detection solution on every joint, including the cylinder valves, regulators, hose ends and torch, and watch for bubbles. Tighten or replace anything that leaks, then purge each hose before lighting.
markingPoints: Cylinders chained upright; valves and outlets clean, with no oil or damage
Regulators checked and fitted with the adjusting screws out; fuel gas left-hand thread
Flashback arrestors at the regulators; hoses inspected; check valves at the torch
Nozzle chosen from the chart and checked; cylinder valves opened slowly, standing aside; pressures set
Every joint leak-tested with solution; leaks fixed; hoses purged before lighting

essays.stem: Compare leftward and rightward oxy-acetylene welding. Describe how each is done, the thickness of steel each suits, and their advantages.
essays.modelAnswer: In leftward welding, also called forehand, a right-handed welder moves from right to left. The flame points forward, towards the part of the joint not yet welded, and the filler rod is held in front of the flame and dipped into the front of the pool. The flame preheats the edges ahead. Leftward welding is used for thin steel sheet, up to about 5 mm. It gives a neat, even finish and good control of a small pool, but on thicker plate it is slow and needs a wide V, so it uses more gas and rod. In rightward welding, also called backhand, the welder moves from left to right. The flame points back at the weld just made, and the rod follows behind the flame, between the flame and the finished weld. Rightward welding is used for steel thicker than about 5 mm. Its advantages are a smaller joint angle, less filler rod and gas, faster welding and good penetration, and the flame shields the hot weld as it cools, which reduces oxidation.
markingPoints: Leftward: flame points forward, rod in front of the flame
Leftward suits thin sheet up to about 5 mm; neat finish and good pool control
Rightward: flame points back at the weld, rod follows behind
Rightward suits steel over about 5 mm
Rightward advantages: smaller joint angle, less rod and gas, faster, good penetration

essays.stem: Explain how you change your technique when welding a butt joint in steel sheet in the vertical-up position, compared with the flat position.
essays.modelAnswer: In the flat position the pool lies on top of the joint and gravity helps it to flow evenly. In the vertical-up position gravity pulls the pool down, so it can sag, run or drip, and undercut can form at the edges. To control this, start at the bottom of the joint and weld upward. Use a nozzle one size smaller than for the flat position, or tilt the torch so that the flame meets the plate at a lower angle, which puts less heat into the pool. Point the flame upward, along the joint, so that the gas pressure helps to hold the pool up. Keep the pool small and add filler rod often at the top edge of the pool, so that the rod helps to support it. Travel steadily and watch that both edges melt, with a slight side-to-side movement to fill the joint without undercut. Place the tacks close together, because the heat builds up as you move up the sheet, and rest your arm to keep the torch steady.
markingPoints: Explains gravity: the pool can sag or drip in the vertical position
Welds upward from the bottom with the flame pointing up the joint
Less heat: a smaller nozzle or a lower flame angle
Keeps the pool small; adds rod at the top edge to support it
Steady travel with both edges fused, no undercut; close tacks and a steady arm

essays.stem: Describe how to make a butt weld in steel sheet in the overhead position, safely and with good quality.
essays.modelAnswer: Overhead welding needs extra care, because hot metal and sparks can fall onto the welder. Wear full PPE: goggles, a cap or hood, a buttoned-up collar, leather sleeves or a jacket, gauntlet gloves and boots, with trousers over the boots. Clear anything that can burn from below the work. Set the job at a height where you can reach the whole joint comfortably, and stand to one side of the joint, not directly under it. Clamp or tack the sheets securely, with tacks close together. Use a slightly smaller nozzle than for flat welding, and a neutral flame. Keep the pool small, because surface tension can hold a small pool up but a large one will drop. Point the flame slightly in the direction of travel and add the rod often to support the pool, keeping its hot end in the outer flame. Travel steadily so that both edges fuse without the pool sagging. Rest your arm when needed, and stop before you get tired, because a shaking hand spoils the weld.
markingPoints: Full PPE including a cap or hood and buttoned collar; anything that can burn cleared from below
Comfortable working height; stands to one side, not directly under the joint
Close tacks; slightly smaller nozzle; neutral flame
Small pool held by surface tension; rod added often to support it
Steady travel with both edges fused; rests to keep the torch steady

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare, tack and weld a small-bore steel pipe butt joint in the fixed horizontal (5G) position with oxy-acetylene.
essays.modelAnswer: Cut both pipe ends square and check them with a square or a wraparound. Prepare the ends as the procedure says: thin-wall pipe can be left square-edged, and thicker wall is bevelled. Clean the ends inside and out to bright metal for about 25 mm. Line the two pipes up on a piece of angle iron or in a jig so that they are straight, with an even root gap all round. Tack the joint in three or four places, evenly spaced, and check the line-up again. Clamp the pipe in a stand with its axis horizontal at a comfortable height; it must not be turned during welding. Use a neutral flame and the nozzle size from the chart. Weld each half uphill, starting just past the bottom (6 o'clock) and finishing just past the top (12 o'clock), changing your body and torch position as you go round so the flame and rod stay at the right angles. Fuse into the tacks, keep the penetration even, and overlap the starts and finishes of the two halves. Clean and inspect the weld.
markingPoints: Ends cut square, prepared (square or bevelled as the procedure says) and cleaned
Pipes lined up straight with an even root gap; three or four evenly spaced tacks
Pipe fixed horizontally in a stand and not turned
Neutral flame; each half welded uphill from bottom to top, changing position to keep the angles
Tacks fused, even penetration, starts and finishes overlapped; weld cleaned and inspected

essays.stem: Name three common defects in oxy-acetylene welds. For each one, give the cause and how to prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Lack of fusion is where the weld metal lies on the edge of the plate without melting into it. It is caused by too little heat, a nozzle that is too small, travel that is too fast, or melting the rod onto cold metal. Prevent it by using the right nozzle, watching that both edges melt into the pool, and adding the rod into the pool, not ahead of it. Burn-through is a hole melted right through the joint. It is caused by too much heat, a nozzle that is too big, a gap that is too wide or travel that is too slow. Prevent it by using the right nozzle from the chart, setting the gap correctly and travelling at a steady speed. Porosity is small gas holes in the weld. It is caused by dirt, rust, paint or oil on the joint, or by an oxidising flame. Prevent it by cleaning back to bright metal and using a neutral flame. Other defects include undercut, from too much heat or a poor torch angle, and cracks.
markingPoints: First defect named, with a correct cause
Correct prevention for the first defect
Second defect named, with a correct cause and prevention
Third defect named, with a correct cause
Correct prevention for the third defect

essays.stem: Explain how an oxy-acetylene test weld is inspected and tested, from the visual check to bend tests.
essays.modelAnswer: First the weld is cleaned and checked by eye, with a magnifying glass if needed. The face should be even in width and height, with even ripples, and should blend smoothly into the plate. There should be no undercut, cracks, porosity, overlap or unfilled crater. The back of a butt weld should show an even penetration bead along its full length, with no burn-through. Sizes are checked with a rule or a weld gauge. Then destructive tests are done on strips cut across the weld. In a face bend test the strip is bent around a former with the face of the weld on the outside; in a root bend test the root is on the outside. A good weld bends without cracking or opening up, which shows good fusion and penetration. In a nick-break (fracture) test, a strip is cut with a small notch in the weld and broken, so that the inside can be checked for gas holes, lack of fusion and other faults. The results are recorded on the test sheet.
markingPoints: Visual check: even face, no undercut, cracks, porosity or crater
Back of a butt weld: even penetration bead, no burn-through; sizes checked with a gauge
Strips cut across the weld for bend tests
Face and root bends explained; a good weld bends without cracking
Nick-break (fracture) test shows inside faults; results recorded

essays.stem: Explain the main differences when gas welding cast iron, or braze welding steel, compared with fusion welding mild steel.
essays.modelAnswer: When fusion welding mild steel, the edges and the filler rod are melted together with a neutral flame, and no flux is needed. Cast iron is brittle and cracks easily if it is heated or cooled unevenly. So the whole casting is preheated slowly, in a furnace or with a large heating nozzle, and kept hot while it is welded. A cast iron filler rod and a cast iron flux are used, with a neutral flame. After welding, the casting is cooled very slowly, for example under an insulating blanket or buried in dry sand or lime. Braze welding (bronze welding) joins steel without melting it. The joint is heated to a red heat, well below the melting point of the steel, and a brass or bronze filler rod is used with a brazing flux and a slightly oxidising flame. The bronze wets (tins) the hot steel surface and bonds to it, and then the joint is built up. It is used for joining thin steel, cast iron and different metals with less heat and distortion. Good ventilation is needed because of the fumes.
markingPoints: Mild steel: edges and rod fused with a neutral flame, no flux
Cast iron: whole casting preheated slowly and kept hot
Cast iron: cast iron rod and flux; cooled very slowly (blanket, dry sand or lime)
Braze welding: steel heated but not melted; brass or bronze rod with flux; slightly oxidising flame
Bronze wets (tins) and bonds to the surface; less heat and distortion; ventilation for fumes

essays.stem: Explain what a flashback is, how flashbacks are prevented, and what you should do if one happens.
essays.modelAnswer: A flashback is when the flame burns back through the nozzle into the torch and may travel into the hoses, the regulators or even the cylinder. You may hear a squealing or hissing sound, see smoke or sparks at the nozzle, and feel the torch handle get hot. It is very dangerous because it can cause a fire or an explosion. Flashbacks are prevented by fitting flashback arrestors at the regulators and check valves at the torch, purging the hoses before lighting so that no mixed gas is left in them, using the correct pressures from the maker's chart, keeping the nozzle clean and tight, not touching the nozzle on the work, and lighting the torch in the right order. If a flashback happens, shut both torch valves at once, in the order the maker's instructions give, then close both cylinder valves. Let the torch cool, and do not use the equipment again until it has been checked. Report it to the instructor. If a cylinder gets hot, clear the area, raise the alarm and call the fire service.
markingPoints: Flashback explained (flame burns back into the torch, hoses or regulators) with signs: squeal, hiss, hot handle
Prevention: flashback arrestors and check valves
Prevention: purging, correct pressures, clean tight nozzle, correct lighting order
Action: shut the torch valves at once (as the maker says), then the cylinder valves
Not reused until checked; reported; clear the area and call the fire service if a cylinder gets hot

practical1.title: Vertical-up (3G) butt weld on 3 mm steel sheet, with a root bend test
practical1.brief: Each member of the group welds one butt joint in 3 mm mild steel sheet in the vertical-up position (3G) with oxy-acetylene, using the leftward method. Two pieces about 150 mm × 50 mm are cleaned, set with the root gap the instructor gives, and tacked, then fixed upright in a positioner or clamp. The group sets up and leak-tests the outfit together, and members take turns at the welding stations while the others check the flames and keep the area safe. When the welds are cool, each member cuts a 25 mm strip from the middle of their weld, using the method the Centre allows, and bends it in a vice with the root on the outside (a root bend). Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Oxy-acetylene outfits with flashback arrestors and check valves (two welding stations)
Welding nozzles to suit 3 mm steel from the maker's chart, tip cleaners and a spark lighter
Two pieces of 3 mm mild steel sheet, about 150 mm × 50 mm, for each member
Copper-coated mild steel filler rod, of the size the instructor gives
A positioner or clamp to hold the test piece upright
Wire brush, file, tongs, vice and a heavy hammer
photos: The outfit set up and leak-tested, with the group in PPE
A member's test piece cleaned and tacked with an even gap
The test piece fixed upright, with a member welding upward
The finished weld face of each member's piece
The back of each weld, showing the penetration bead
Each member's bent strip, root side out
The area cleaned and the outfit shut down
checklist: Wore full PPE, with gas welding goggles of a suitable shade
Took part in checking and leak-testing the outfit
Set a neutral flame with the right nozzle from the chart
Cleaned, gapped and tacked the joint correctly
Welded upward with a small, controlled pool, adding rod into the pool
Weld face even, with no undercut, holes or sagging; even penetration on the back
Root bend strip bent without cracking or opening along the weld
Shut down correctly and left the area safe and clean
safety: Cylinders chained upright; leak-test before lighting; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Clear anything that can burn; keep an extinguisher at hand
Hang the torch up when not in use; never leave it lit
Treat test pieces as hot: use tongs and mark them HOT
Wear safety glasses and a face shield when cutting or bending the strips

practical2.title: Fixed horizontal (5G) butt weld on small-bore steel pipe
practical2.brief: Each member of the group prepares and welds one butt joint between two short lengths of small-bore mild steel pipe (about 50–60 mm outside diameter, with a wall about 3 mm thick) in the fixed horizontal position (5G) with oxy-acetylene. Each member checks the ends are square, prepares and cleans them as the instructor's procedure says, sets the root gap, tacks the joint in three or four places, and clamps it in the stand with its axis horizontal at chest height. Weld each half uphill from the bottom to the top without turning the pipe. The group shares the welding stations; members who are not welding help to check the line-up, watch the area and keep a log of who welded each joint. When the joints are cool, the group inspects every joint and the instructor cuts one section through a joint so that the penetration can be seen. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Oxy-acetylene outfits with flashback arrestors and check valves
Welding nozzles from the maker's chart, tip cleaners and a spark lighter
Two lengths of mild steel pipe, about 50–60 mm outside diameter and 100 mm long, for each member
Pipe stand or positioner, angle iron for lining up, and clamps
File, wire brush, wraparound, square and tongs
photos: The pipe ends prepared and cleaned
The pipes lined up on angle iron with an even gap
The joint tacked in three or four places
The pipe fixed horizontally in the stand, with a member welding uphill
Each member's finished joint, showing the weld all round the pipe
The cut section through a joint, showing the penetration
The area cleaned and the outfit shut down
checklist: Wore full PPE, including a cap and buttoned collar for the overhead part
Prepared and cleaned the pipe ends as the procedure says
Lined up the pipes straight with an even gap, and tacked them evenly
Kept the pipe fixed and welded each half uphill from bottom to top
Changed body and torch position to keep the flame and rod angles right
Weld even all round, with tacks fused in and starts and finishes overlapped
No burn-through, undercut or holes; even penetration where it can be seen
Shut down correctly and left the area safe and clean
safety: Cylinders chained upright; leak-test before lighting; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Keep hoses away from hot pipe and falling sparks
Never stand directly under the joint when welding the top part
Treat pipes as hot after welding: use tongs and mark them HOT
Keep an extinguisher at hand and the area clear of anything that can burn
